# The Vanishing Night

There is a species of darkness that most people alive today have never met. Not the soft gloom behind closed eyelids, not the cozy dimness of a bedroom with the curtains drawn, but planetary night — the darkness that settles when you are hours from the nearest town, when the last generator goes quiet, and the sky opens overhead like something poured rather than hung. People who stumble into it, usually by accident, tend to describe the encounter in the language of religion. They say they felt small. They say they felt watched. Most often they say, with genuine bewilderment, that they had no idea. No idea that the night contained so much. No idea that the day had been hiding it from them.

For nearly the whole span of human history, this darkness was simply the second half of every life. Our ancestors did not experience night as an interruption of the day but as a place they went, nightly, whether they wished to or not — a country with its own weather, its own customs, its own dangers and graces. The historian Roger Ekirch spent years digging through diaries, court records, letters, and medical texts from the centuries before electrification, and what he found overturned a comfortable assumption: that people once slept the way we imagine we're supposed to, one long unconscious stretch from dusk to dawn. They didn't. They slept in two shifts. There was a "first sleep," begun shortly after evening prayers, and then, around midnight, a gentle return to wakefulness that lasted an hour or more — a period contemporaries called "the watch" — followed by a "second sleep" that carried them to morning.

That middle hour was nobody's insomnia. Documents refer to it casually, without alarm, the way we might mention getting up for a glass of water. People prayed; the interval was considered especially suited to contemplation, and devotional manuals gave instructions for it. They talked. Husbands and wives, lying in the dark, appear to have done some of their best confiding there. They reviewed their dreams, which were taken seriously as correspondence from elsewhere. Some got up and tended the fire, mended a tool, checked on livestock, or — Ekirch found records suggesting this happened more than once — slipped down the lane to visit a neighbor. Sleep, for most of our species' tenure on Earth, was a braid, not a rope.

Night was also the other half of the mind. Daylight belonged to work and negotiation; darkness belonged to imagination, and everyone knew it. Stories were told after sundown, around fires, in the long seasons when the lamp oil ran low, and the stories were shaped by their setting — full of travelers who took wrong roads, of voices in hedges, of the dead who walked. Ghosts are creatures of the pre-electric world for a reason. The dark was a canvas, and we painted on it everything we feared and half-believed, which is to say most of what we knew. A child raised on such nights learned early that reality had layers, and that some of them only showed themselves when the light went out.

Yet the old night had teeth, and it's worth being honest about them. Darkness was expensive. A laborer who lit a tallow candle after sundown was, quite literally, burning wages; rushlights — dried rushes dipped in animal fat — gave off a smoky, guttering glow because they were what the poor could afford. Clean-burning spermaceti candles belonged to people with money. Night was when thieves worked, when the road between villages became genuinely perilous, when curfew bells rang and city gates closed. The watchman with his lantern and his call was not picturesque; he was infrastructure. Fear of the dark is not a childish superstition. It is a fossil of very reasonable ancestral caution.

So when light came, it came as liberation, and it came fast, historically speaking. Gas pipes threaded through London in the 1810s and 1820s; Paris earned its nickname; arc lamps blazed over American streets in the 1880s, startling horses; and then Edison's Pearl Street station began feeding current to a square mile of Manhattan in 1882, and the second sun switched on. Within a century the transformation was total. Night, which had been a wall, became a curtain — thin, optional, easily pushed aside. We extended the working day, the school day, the shopping day, the self. Whatever else we say about it, this was one of the great liberations of the species, and it would be sentimental to pretend otherwise. Surgeons operate at three in the morning. A mother reads to her child in a warm pool of lamplight. The emergency room never closes. Much of what we love about modern life happens after dark.

But every liberation has a ledger, and we have been slow to read the debit column. Consider what may be among the strangest statistics of the age: according to a global atlas of artificial sky brightness published in *Science Advances* in 2016, more than eighty percent of North Americans — and roughly a third of all humans — can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. Not obscured, not dimmed: gone, erased behind a dome of scattered light called skyglow, which turns the night sky a featureless gray-orange above most cities and suburbs. The galaxy that every human being who ever lived before us knew intimately — that named their months, steered their ships, housed their gods and their dead — has become, within four generations, a rumor.

This is worth pausing on, because the loss is stranger than prettiness foregone. The night sky was the first shared text of our species. Long before writing, people read it. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific holding star paths in memory, rising stars as signposts, swells and birds as corroboration. Farmers planted by the Pleiades. Egyptian priests timed the Nile's flood to the heliacal rising of Sirius. Every culture that left us any record at all left constellations — bear and hunter, river and serpent — proof that looking up and finding figures in the dark is something human beings simply do, the way we find faces in wood grain. Kant wrote that two things filled him with ever-growing awe: the moral law within and the starry heavens above. He could assume his readers had recently seen the second one. We cannot.

And the damage does not stop at the edge of the atmosphere. Light pollution is not merely an aesthetic complaint; it is an ecological force, and the evidence has been accumulating for decades. On beaches in Florida, sea turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests at night and instinctively crawl toward the brighter horizon — which, for a hundred million years, meant the sea, moonlit and starlit, reflecting more light than the dark land behind. Now the brightest horizon is often a strip of beachfront hotels, and thousands of hatchlings march inland, toward patios and parking lots, to die of exhaustion, dehydration, or traffic. Several coastal counties now regulate beachfront lighting during nesting season, dimming our lights so that an older light can do its work.

Birds fare no better. Roughly two-thirds of migratory songbirds travel at night, navigating by stars and by cues we still don't fully understand, and city towers lit up like flares draw them into lethal confusion. In October 2023, nearly a thousand birds died in a single night colliding with one lakeside convention center in Chicago — a building whose lights, on a foggy night along a migration route, had become a trap. When New York periodically dims the Tribute in Light memorial, researchers have shown, the thousands of birds circling inside those beams disperse within minutes. The remedy is almost embarrassingly simple: turn the lights off, or point them down. The birds resume their journey as though released from a spell.

Moths, meanwhile, are living out a tragedy we barely notice. The prevailing theory holds that they navigate by holding a fixed angle to a distant light source — the moon — which works beautifully until the light source is thirty inches away and attached to your porch. Circling becomes spiraling; the strategy that served them for millions of years becomes a death dance around a bulb. Multiply that porch light by hundreds of millions of streetlamps, billboards, and shop windows, add the finding that insect populations are declining worldwide for reasons that include habitat loss and pesticides, and you begin to see the night as what it really is: not an absence covering half the planet, but a habitat — one we have been draining the way we drained the wetlands, without much thought to what lived there. Even fireflies, whose entire love language is light, are going quiet in glowing suburbs; their flashes cannot compete, and their courtship fails in the noise.

Nor is the problem confined to land. The largest habitat on Earth is already dark: sunlight penetrates only the top two hundred meters of the ocean, and everything below — the overwhelming majority of the biosphere's livable volume — runs on no light but its own. Anglerfish dangle their lures; lanternfish wear rows of glowing ports; whole families of creatures make their own weather of sparks. And the greatest migration on Earth happens every single night, when trillions of animals — plankton, squid, small fish — rise from the depths toward the surface under cover of darkness to feed, then sink again before dawn. Off brightly lit coastlines, researchers have found, this ancient commute frays: plankton that should rise stay down, and food webs wobble. Even the sea's night is thinning.

Our own bodies keep the old calendar, too. In the early 2000s, researchers identified cells in the retina — intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells — that don't help us see at all. Their job is to tell the brain what time it is, and they are exquisitely tuned to the blue wavelengths of daylight. When they report "day," the pineal gland withholds melatonin; when they fall silent, the hormone flows and sleep chemistry begins. This system calibrated itself across millions of years of bright days and truly dark nights. It has had about a century and a half to adjust to indoor life, and it hasn't. We spend our days in offices too dim to give the clock a firm noon, and our evenings bathed in screens emitting precisely the wavelengths that say *morning*. The result is a peculiar modern twilight: chronically under-lit by day, over-lit by night, our internal clocks drifting like unmoored boats.

The costs show up in the data. The World Health Organization's cancer agency classifies shift work that disrupts circadian rhythms as a probable human carcinogen — a startling phrase to attach to a schedule. Nurses, flight crews, and factory workers on rotating shifts show elevated rates of metabolic disease, depression, and certain cancers. Hospital nurseries run so brightly that newborns must somehow be taught that night exists. Among the elderly, the yellowing lens of the eye filters out exactly the blue light the circadian clock depends on, contributing to the fragmented sleep and disorientation so common in late life. We built a world without night and then wondered why our bodies kept insisting on one.

None of this argues for dismantling the grid, and nobody serious is proposing to. Light is not the enemy; careless light is. The distinction matters. A streetlamp that throws half its output upward into the sky illuminates nothing but the bellies of clouds. Shielded fixtures, warmer color temperatures, motion sensors, timers, ordinances requiring lights to be aimed where they're needed — these preserve safety while giving the dark back its territory. Flagstaff, Arizona, figured this out generations ago; home to major observatories, it adopted strict lighting codes beginning in the late 1950s and became the world's first International Dark Sky City in 2001, demonstrating that a town of seventy thousand people can keep its streets safe and its sky legible at the same time.

Since the International Dark-Sky Association was founded in 1988, dozens of parks and reserves around the world have been certified for their darkness, and a modest trade in astro-tourism has grown up around them. What strikes you in the accounts of visitors is not the astronomy but the emotion. People cry at the Milky Way. Guides at dark-sky sites report it routinely: adults, seeing the galaxy clearly for the first time since childhood — or for the first time ever — standing in silence, some of them weeping, unable to explain why. Psychologists studying awe have found that experiences of vastness reliably shrink the sense of self, and that this shrinking, counterintuitively, leaves people feeling more connected to others and more generous. The night sky may be the cheapest awe available to our species. We have been spending it like it was nothing.

Here is the part I keep returning to: darkness is not nothing. It is not the mere absence of light, a blank page, a zero. It is a medium, and things live in it. Sit somewhere truly dark and give your eyes twenty minutes — the time it takes for rhodopsin, the pigment of rod vision, to regenerate — and the world reassembles itself around you. Stars that weren't there arrive by the hundred, then the thousand. You begin to see what astronomers prize in pristine skies: the faint cone of zodiacal light, the ghostly green shimmer of airglow near the horizon, the Milky Way resolved from haze into individual flames. Sounds sharpen; the ear takes up the slack. You notice your own breathing. The dark is not empty. It is full, and it was full all along, and only the light was missing.

I think of a summer power outage years ago — the whole grid down, the whole neighborhood spilled into the streets at ten at night, blinking upward. Someone said, quietly, "Look." And there it was, the Milky Way, arched over the rooftops of a suburb that hadn't seen it in fifty years, over lawns and driveways and parked cars, patient as a letter that had finally been opened. Strangers stood together in the dark pointing at it, telling their children the names of things they themselves were only half sure of. The power came back around midnight, the streetlights snapped on, and the sky closed like a book. Everyone felt the loss. Nobody quite knew what to call it.

Maybe that is the right name for what we owe the night: not nostalgia, which wants the past back, but attention, which wants the present enlarged. We will not give up our illuminated evenings, nor should we. But we can leave a door open. Turn off the porch light one clear night a month. Drive forty minutes past the last highway interchange. Give your eyes their twenty minutes and let the old text resolve. Somewhere in the dark, the same stars that steered the canoes are waiting — the same light that fell on every ancestor who ever looked up, falling on us all along, patiently, asking almost nothing except that we occasionally look.

# The Vanishing Night

There is a species of darkness that most people alive today have never met. Not the soft gloom behind closed eyelids, not the cozy dimness of a bedroom with the curtains drawn, but planetary night — the darkness that settles when you are hours from the nearest town, when the last generator goes quiet, and the sky opens overhead like something poured rather than hung. People who stumble into it, usually by accident, tend to describe the encounter in the language of religion. They say they felt small. They say they felt watched. Most often they say, with genuine bewilderment, that they had no idea. No idea that the night contained so much. No idea that the day had been hiding it from them.

(~130 words)

For nearly the whole span of human history, this darkness was simply the second half of every life. Our ancestors did not experience night as an interruption of the day but as a place they went, nightly, whether they wished to or not — a country with its own weather, its own customs, its own dangers and graces. The historian Roger Ekirch spent years digging through diaries, court records, letters, and medical texts from the centuries before electrification, and what he found overturned a comfortable assumption: that people once slept the way we imagine we're supposed to, one long unconscious stretch from dusk to dawn. They didn't. They slept in two shifts. There was a "first sleep," begun shortly after evening prayers, and then, around midnight, a gentle return to wakefulness that lasted an hour or more — a period contemporaries called "the watch" — followed by a "second sleep" that carried them to morning.

(~160)

That middle hour was nobody's insomnia. Documents refer to it casually, without alarm, the way we might mention getting up for a glass of water. People prayed; the interval was considered especially suited to contemplation, and devotional manuals gave instructions for it. They talked. Husbands and wives, lying in the dark, appear to have done some of their best confiding there. They reviewed their dreams, which were taken seriously as correspondence from elsewhere. Some got up and tended the fire, mended a tool, checked on livestock, or — Ekirch found records suggesting this happened more than once — slipped down the lane to visit a neighbor. Sleep, for most of our species' tenure on Earth, was a braid, not a rope.

(~130)

Yet the old night had teeth, and it's worth being honest about them. Darkness was expensive. A laborer who lit a tallow candle after sundown was, quite literally, burning wages; rushlights — dried rushes dipped in animal fat — gave off a smoky, guttering light because they were what the poor could afford. Spermaceti candles, clean and bright, belonged to people with money. Night was when thieves worked, when the road between villages became genuinely perilous, when curfews rang and gates closed and cities locked themselves in. The watchman with his lantern and his call was not picturesque; he was infrastructure. Fear of the dark is not a childish superstition. It is a fossil of very reasonable ancestral caution.

(~125)

So when light came, it came as liberation, and it came fast, historically speaking. Gas pipelines threaded London in the 1810s and 1820s; Paris earned its nickname; arc lamps blazed over American streets in the 1880s, startling horses; and then Edison's Pearl Street station began feeding current to a square mile of Manhattan in 1882, and the second sun switched on. Within a century, the transformation was total. Night, which had been a wall, became a curtain — thin, optional, easily pushed aside. We extended the working day, the school day, the shopping day, the self. Whatever else we say about it, this was one of the great liberations of the species, and it would be sentimental to pretend otherwise. Surgeons operate at three in the morning. A mother reads to her child in a warm pool of lamplight. The emergency room never closes. Much of what we love about modern life happens after dark.

(~150)

But every liberation has a ledger, and we have been slow to read the debit column. Consider what may be the strangest statistic of the age: according to a global atlas of artificial sky brightness published in Science Advances in 2016, more than eighty percent of North Americans — and roughly a third of all humans — can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. Not obscured, not dimmed: gone, erased behind a dome of scattered light called skyglow, which turns the night sky a featureless gray-orange above most cities and suburbs. The galaxy that every human being who ever lived before us knew intimately — that named their months, steered their ships, housed their gods and their dead — has become, within four generations, a rumor.

(~135)

This is worth pausing on, because the loss is stranger than mere prettiness foregone. The night sky was the first shared text of our species. Long before writing, people read it. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific holding star paths in memory, rising stars as signposts, swells and birds as corroboration. Farmers planted by the Pleiades. Egyptian priests timed the Nile's flood to the heliacal rising of Sirius. Every culture that left us any record at all left constellations — bear and hunter, river and serpent — proof that looking up and finding figures in the dark is something human beings simply do, the way we find faces in wood grain. Kant wrote that two things filled him with ever-growing awe: the moral law within and the starry heavens above. He could assume his readers had recently seen the second one. We cannot.

(~150)

And the damage doesn't stop at the edge of the atmosphere. Light pollution is not just an aesthetic complaint; it is an ecological force, and the evidence has been accumulating for decades. On beaches in Florida, sea turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests at night and instinctively crawl toward the brighter horizon — which, for a hundred million years, meant the sea, moonlit and starlit, reflecting more light than the dark land behind. Now the brightest horizon is often a strip of beachfront hotels, and thousands of hatchlings march inland, toward patios and parking lots, to die of exhaustion, dehydration, or traffic. Several coastal counties now regulate beachfront lighting during nesting season, dimming our lights so that an older light can do its work.

(~120)

Birds fare no better. Roughly two-thirds of migratory songbirds travel at night, navigating by stars and by subtle cues we still don't fully understand, and city towers lit up like flares draw them into lethal confusion. In October 2023, nearly a thousand birds died in a single night colliding with one lakeside convention center in Chicago — a building whose lights, on a foggy night along a migration route, had become a trap. When New York dims the Tribute in Light memorial for periodic intervals, researchers have shown, the thousands of birds circling inside those beams disperse within minutes. The remedy is almost embarrassingly simple: turn the lights off, or point them down. The birds resume their journey as though released from a spell.

(~125)

Moths, meanwhile, are living out a tragedy we barely notice. The prevailing theory holds that they navigate by maintaining a fixed angle to a distant light source — the moon — which works beautifully until the light source is thirty inches away and attached to your porch. Circling becomes spiraling; the strategy that served them for millions of years becomes a death dance around a bulb. Multiply that porch light by hundreds of millions of streetlamps, billboards, and shop windows, add the finding that insects are declining worldwide for reasons that include habitat loss and pesticides, and you begin to see the night as what it is: not an absence covering half the planet, but a habitat — one we have been draining the way we drained the wetlands, without much thought to what lived there. Even fireflies, whose entire love language is light, are going quiet in glowing suburbs; their flashes cannot compete, and their courtship fails in the noise.

(~155)

Our own bodies keep the old calendar, too. In the early 2000s, researchers identified cells in the retina — intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells — that don't help us see at all. Their job is to tell the brain what time it is, and they are exquisitely tuned to the blue wavelengths of daylight. When they report "day," the pineal gland withholds melatonin; when they stop reporting, the hormone flows and sleep chemistry begins. This system calibrated itself across millions of years of bright days and truly dark nights. It has had about a century and a half to adjust to indoor life, and it hasn't. We spend our days in offices too dim to give the clock a firm noon, and our evenings bathed in screens emitting precisely the wavelengths that say morning. The result is a peculiar modern twilight: chronically under-lit by day, over-lit by night, our internal clocks drifting like unmoored boats.

(~155)

The costs show up in the data. The World Health Organization's cancer agency classified shift work that disrupts circadian rhythms as a probable human carcinogen — a startling phrase for a schedule. Nurses and flight crews and factory workers on rotating shifts show elevated rates of metabolic disease, depression, and certain cancers. Hospital nurseries run so brightly that newborns must be taught, in effect, that night exists. And among the elderly, the yellowing lens of the eye filters out exactly the blue light the circadian clock needs, contributing to the fragmented sleep and disorientation so common in late life. We built a world without night and then wondered why our bodies kept insisting on one.

(~115)

None of this argues for dismantling the grid, and the good news is that nobody serious is proposing to. Light is not the enemy; careless light is. The distinction matters. A streetlamp that throws half its output upward into the sky illuminates nothing but the bellies of clouds. Shielded fixtures, warmer color temperatures, motion sensors, timers, ordinances that require lights to be aimed where they're needed — these preserve safety while giving the dark back its territory. The city of Flagstaff, Arizona, figured this out decades ago; home to major observatories, it adopted strict lighting codes in the 1950s and became the world's first International Dark Sky City in 2001, proving that a town of seventy thousand can keep its streets safe and its sky legible at the same time.

(~130)

Since the International Dark-Sky Association was founded in 1988, dozens of parks and reserves around the world have been certified for their darkness, and a modest industry of astro-tourism has grown up around them. What's striking in the accounts of visitors is not the astronomy but the emotion. People cry at the Milky Way. Guides at dark-sky sites report it routinely: adults, seeing the galaxy clearly for the first time since childhood — or for the first time ever — standing in silence, some of them weeping, unable to explain why. Psychologists studying awe have found that experiences of vastness reliably shrink the sense of self, and that this shrinking, counterintuitively, makes people feel more connected to others and more generous. The night sky may be the cheapest awe available to our species. We have been spending it like it was nothing.

(~140)

Here is the part I keep returning to: darkness is not nothing. It is not the mere absence of light, a blank page, a zero. It is a medium, and things live in it. Sit somewhere truly dark and give your eyes twenty minutes — the time it takes for rhodopsin, the pigment of rod vision, to regenerate fully — and the world reassembles itself around you. Stars that weren't there arrive by the hundred, then the thousand. You begin to see what astronomers prize in pristine skies: the faint band of the zodiacal light, the ghostly airglow that shimmers green near the horizon, the Milky Way resolved from haze into individual flames. Sounds sharpen; the ear takes up the slack. You notice your own breathing. The dark is not empty. It is full, and it was full all along, and only the light was missing.

(~145)

I think of a summer power outage years ago — the whole grid down, the whole neighborhood spilled into the streets at ten at night, blinking upward. Someone said, quietly, "Look." And there it was, the Milky Way, arched over the rooftops of a suburb that hadn't seen it in fifty years, over lawns and driveways and parked cars, patient as a letter that had finally been opened. Strangers stood together in the dark pointing at it, telling their children the names of things they themselves were only half sure of. The power came back around midnight, and the streetlights snapped on, and the sky closed like a book. Everyone felt the loss. Nobody quite knew what to call it.

(~120)

Maybe that's the right name for what we owe the night: not nostalgia, which wants the past back, but attention, which wants the present enlarged. We will not give up our illuminated evenings, nor should we. But we can leave a door open. Turn off the porch light one clear night a month. Drive forty minutes past the last interchange. Give your eyes their twenty minutes and let the old text resolve. Somewhere in the dark, the same stars that steered the canoes are waiting, the same light that fell on every ancestor who ever looked up — and it has been falling on us all along, patiently, all this time, asking almost nothing except that we occasionally look.

# The Vanishing Night

There is a species of darkness that most people alive today have never met. Not the soft gloom behind closed eyelids, not the cozy dimness of a bedroom with the curtains drawn, but planetary night — the darkness that settles when you are hours from the nearest town, when the last generator goes quiet, and the sky opens overhead like something poured rather than hung. People who stumble into it, usually by accident, tend to describe the encounter in the language of religion. They say they felt small. They say they felt watched. Most often they say, with genuine bewilderment, that they had no idea. No idea that the night contained so much. No idea that the day had been hiding it from them.

(~130 words)

For nearly the whole span of human history, this darkness was simply the second half of every life. Our ancestors did not experience night as an interruption of the day but as a place they went, nightly, whether they wished to or not — a country with its own weather, its own customs, its own dangers and graces. The historian Roger Ekirch spent years digging through diaries, court records, letters, and medical texts from the centuries before electrification, and what he found overturned a comfortable assumption: that people once slept the way we imagine we're supposed to, one long unconscious stretch from dusk to dawn. They didn't. They slept in two shifts. There was a "first sleep," begun shortly after evening prayers, and then, around midnight, a gentle return to wakefulness that lasted an hour or more — a period contemporaries called "the watch" — followed by a "second sleep" that carried them to morning.

(~160)

That middle hour was nobody's insomnia. Documents refer to it casually, without alarm, the way we might mention getting up for a glass of water. People prayed; the interval was considered especially suited to contemplation, and devotional manuals gave instructions for it. They talked. Husbands and wives, lying in the dark, appear to have done some of their best confiding there. They reviewed their dreams, which were taken seriously as correspondence from elsewhere. Some got up and tended the fire, mended a tool, checked on livestock, or — Ekirch found records suggesting this happened more than once — slipped down the lane to visit a neighbor. Sleep, for most of our species' tenure on Earth, was a braid, not a rope.

(~130)

Yet the old night had teeth, and it's worth being honest about them. Darkness was expensive. A laborer who lit a tallow candle after sundown was, quite literally, burning wages; rushlights — dried rushes dipped in animal fat — gave off a smoky, guttering light because they were what the poor could afford. Spermaceti candles, clean and bright, belonged to people with money. Night was when thieves worked, when the road between villages became genuinely perilous, when curfews rang and gates closed and cities locked themselves in. The watchman with his lantern and his call was not picturesque; he was infrastructure. Fear of the dark is not a childish superstition. It is a fossil of very reasonable ancestral caution.

(~125)

So when light came, it came as liberation, and it came fast, historically speaking. Gas pipelines threaded London in the 1810s and 1820s; Paris earned its nickname; arc lamps blazed over American streets in the 1880s, startling horses; and then Edison's Pearl Street station began feeding current to a square mile of Manhattan in 1882, and the second sun switched on. Within a century, the transformation was total. Night, which had been a wall, became a curtain — thin, optional, easily pushed aside. We extended the working day, the school day, the shopping day, the self. Whatever else we say about it, this was one of the great liberations of the species, and it would be sentimental to pretend otherwise. Surgeons operate at three in the morning. A mother reads to her child in a warm pool of lamplight. The emergency room never closes. Much of what we love about modern life happens after dark.

(~150)

But every liberation has a ledger, and we have been slow to read the debit column. Consider what may be the strangest statistic of the age: according to a global atlas of artificial sky brightness published in Science Advances in 2016, more than eighty percent of North Americans — and roughly a third of all humans — can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. Not obscured, not dimmed: gone, erased behind a dome of scattered light called skyglow, which turns the night sky a featureless gray-orange above most cities and suburbs. The galaxy that every human being who ever lived before us knew intimately — that named their months, steered their ships, housed their gods and their dead — has become, within four generations, a rumor.

(~135)

This is worth pausing on, because the loss is stranger than mere prettiness foregone. The night sky was the first shared text of our species. Long before writing, people read it. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific holding star paths in memory, rising stars as signposts, swells and birds as corroboration. Farmers planted by the Pleiades. Egyptian priests timed the Nile's flood to the heliacal rising of Sirius. Every culture that left us any record at all left constellations — bear and hunter, river and serpent — proof that looking up and finding figures in the dark is something human beings simply do, the way we find faces in wood grain. Kant wrote that two things filled him with ever-growing awe: the moral law within and the starry heavens above. He could assume his readers had recently seen the second one. We cannot.

(~150)

And the damage doesn't stop at the edge of the atmosphere. Light pollution is not just an aesthetic complaint; it is an ecological force, and the evidence has been accumulating for decades. On beaches in Florida, sea turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests at night and instinctively crawl toward the brighter horizon — which, for a hundred million years, meant the sea, moonlit and starlit, reflecting more light than the dark land behind. Now the brightest horizon is often a strip of beachfront hotels, and thousands of hatchlings march inland, toward patios and parking lots, to die of exhaustion, dehydration, or traffic. Several coastal counties now regulate beachfront lighting during nesting season, dimming our lights so that an older light can do its work.

(~120)

Birds fare no better. Roughly two-thirds of migratory songbirds travel at night, navigating by stars and by subtle cues we still don't fully understand, and city towers lit up like flares draw them into lethal confusion. In October 2023, nearly a thousand birds died in a single night colliding with one lakeside convention center in Chicago — a building whose lights, on a foggy night along a migration route, had become a trap. When New York dims the Tribute in Light memorial for periodic intervals, researchers have shown, the thousands of birds circling inside those beams disperse within minutes. The remedy is almost embarrassingly simple: turn the lights off, or point them down. The birds resume their journey as though released from a spell.

(~125)

Moths, meanwhile, are living out a tragedy we barely notice. The prevailing theory holds that they navigate by maintaining a fixed angle to a distant light source — the moon — which works beautifully until the light source is thirty inches away and attached to your porch. Circling becomes spiraling; the strategy that served them for millions of years becomes a death dance around a bulb. Multiply that porch light by hundreds of millions of streetlamps, billboards, and shop windows, add the finding that insects are declining worldwide for reasons that include habitat loss and pesticides, and you begin to see the night as what it is: not an absence covering half the planet, but a habitat — one we have been draining the way we drained the wetlands, without much thought to what lived there. Even fireflies, whose entire love language is light, are going quiet in glowing suburbs; their flashes cannot compete, and their courtship fails in the noise.

(~155)

Our own bodies keep the old calendar, too. In the early 2000s, researchers identified cells in the retina — intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells — that don't help us see at all. Their job is to tell the brain what time it is, and they are exquisitely tuned to the blue wavelengths of daylight. When they report "day," the pineal gland withholds melatonin; when they stop reporting, the hormone flows and sleep chemistry begins. This system calibrated itself across millions of years of bright days and truly dark nights. It has had about a century and a half to adjust to indoor life, and it hasn't. We spend our days in offices too dim to give the clock a firm noon, and our evenings bathed in screens emitting precisely the wavelengths that say morning. The result is a peculiar modern twilight: chronically under-lit by day, over-lit by night, our internal clocks drifting like unmoored boats.

(~155)

The costs show up in the data. The World Health Organization's cancer agency classified shift work that disrupts circadian rhythms as a probable human carcinogen — a startling phrase for a schedule. Nurses and flight crews and factory workers on rotating shifts show elevated rates of metabolic disease, depression, and certain cancers. Hospital nurseries run so brightly that newborns must be taught, in effect, that night exists. And among the elderly, the yellowing lens of the eye filters out exactly the blue light the circadian clock needs, contributing to the fragmented sleep and disorientation so common in late life. We built a world without night and then wondered why our bodies kept insisting on one.

(~115)

None of this argues for dismantling the grid, and the good news is that nobody serious is proposing to. Light is not the enemy; careless light is. The distinction matters. A streetlamp that throws half its output upward into the sky illuminates nothing but the bellies of clouds. Shielded fixtures, warmer color temperatures, motion sensors, timers, ordinances that require lights to be aimed where they're needed — these preserve safety while giving the dark back its territory. The city of Flagstaff, Arizona, figured this out decades ago; home to major observatories, it adopted strict lighting codes in the 1950s and became the world's first International Dark Sky City in 2001, proving that a town of seventy thousand can keep its streets safe and its sky legible at the same time.

(~130)

Since the International Dark-Sky Association was founded in 1988, dozens of parks and reserves around the world have been certified for their darkness, and a modest industry of astro-tourism has grown up around them. What's striking in the accounts of visitors is not the astronomy but the emotion. People cry at the Milky Way. Guides at dark-sky sites report it routinely: adults, seeing the galaxy clearly for the first time since childhood — or for the first time ever — standing in silence, some of them weeping, unable to explain why. Psychologists studying awe have found that experiences of vastness reliably shrink the sense of self, and that this shrinking, counterintuitively, makes people feel more connected to others and more generous. The night sky may be the cheapest awe available to our species. We have been spending it like it was nothing.

(~140)

Here is the part I keep returning to: darkness is not nothing. It is not the mere absence of light, a blank page, a zero. It is a medium, and things live in it. Sit somewhere truly dark and give your eyes twenty minutes — the time it takes for rhodopsin, the pigment of rod vision, to regenerate fully — and the world reassembles itself around you. Stars that weren't there arrive by the hundred, then the thousand. You begin to see what astronomers prize in pristine skies: the faint band of the zodiacal light, the ghostly airglow that shimmers green near the horizon, the Milky Way resolved from haze into individual flames. Sounds sharpen; the ear takes up the slack. You notice your own breathing. The dark is not empty. It is full, and it was full all along, and only the light was missing.

(~145)

I think of a summer power outage years ago — the whole grid down, the whole neighborhood spilled into the streets at ten at night, blinking upward. Someone said, quietly, "Look." And there it was, the Milky Way, arched over the rooftops of a suburb that hadn't seen it in fifty years, over lawns and driveways and parked cars, patient as a letter that had finally been opened. Strangers stood together in the dark pointing at it, telling their children the names of things they themselves were only half sure of. The power came back around midnight, and the streetlights snapped on, and the sky closed like a book. Everyone felt the loss. Nobody quite knew what to call it.

(~120)

Maybe that's the right name for what we owe the night: not nostalgia, which wants the past back, but attention, which wants the present enlarged. We will not give up our illuminated evenings, nor should we. But we can leave a door open. Turn off the porch light one clear night a month. Drive forty minutes past the last interchange. Give your eyes their twenty minutes and let the old text resolve. Somewhere in the dark, the same stars that steered the canoes are waiting, the same light that fell on every ancestor who ever looked up — and it has been falling on us all along, patiently, all this time, asking almost nothing except that we occasionally look.

(~110)
